title: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT
definition: Instructions that define the default command executed when a container starts. `CMD` provides default arguments that a user can easily override. `ENTRYPOINT` configures a container to run as an unyielding executable.
simpleExplanation:
When the container wakes up, what is its primary job? 
`CMD` is a suggestion: 'When you wake up, run `python main.py`. (But if the user overrides it by typing `bash`, do that instead).'
`ENTRYPOINT` is a strict law: 'When you wake up, you MUST run `python`. If the user passes arguments, append them, but you ARE a python script.'
realWorldExample: An NGINX web server uses `CMD ["nginx", "-g", "daemon off;"]`. When the container starts, the web server boots. But if you want to debug, you can run `docker run -it nginx bash`, completely overriding the CMD and starting a bash shell instead.

basic: If a Dockerfile has five `CMD` instructions scattered throughout it, what happens?
intermediate: How do `CMD` and `ENTRYPOINT` work together in the same Dockerfile?

answers.question: Five CMD instructions?
answers.answer: Docker completely ignores the first four. Only the absolute last `CMD` instruction in the file will take effect.

answers.question: Work together?
answers.answer:
If you use both, `ENTRYPOINT` becomes the un-changeable executable, and `CMD` becomes the default arguments fed into it. 
Example: 
`ENTRYPOINT ["ping"]`
`CMD ["google.com"]`
By default, it pings google. If the user types `docker run myimage yahoo.com`, it overrides the CMD and pings yahoo instead.
